title: Identity, Governance & Shipping Code
subtitle: Principals, securables, privileges, dev→staging→prod, Git, CI/CD, IaC, Bundles — and the three classic debugging cases
mantra: Know WHO is running, WHAT it may touch and HOW the code reached prod — then debug by finding the first layer where reality diverges from what you expected.
objectives: You can separate authentication from authorization and name the three principal types.
You can read a GRANT statement word by word and list every privilege needed to SELECT from catalog.schema.table.
You can debug PERMISSION_DENIED in the right order — ending with 'which identity is ACTUALLY running?'.
You can explain least privilege and why ALL PRIVILEGES for everybody is a bad fix.
You can describe dev → test/staging → prod, Git flow, CI, CD and Infrastructure as Code (Declarative Automation Bundles, formerly Asset Bundles).
You can run the three classic debugging playbooks: no new data, duplicate records, works in dev / fails in prod.
You can map the whole platform: Lakeflow/Spark, Unity Catalog, Git/CI/CD, Bundles, Delta + cloud storage.

sections.title: Authentication vs Authorization
sections.hook: 'Who are you?' and 'What may you do?' are two different questions — and two different failure modes.

items.title: Authentication
points: System proves: this really is Nikos

items.title: Authorization
points: Question: **What are you allowed to do?**

head: Action by Nikos
Allowed?
blocks.caption: Authorization = a list of allowed actions for a known identity

blocks.title: Hotel analogy
blocks.text: Reception checks your passport — **authentication**. Your key card then opens only your room and the gym, not the kitchen — **authorization**.

blocks.title: Order matters
blocks.text: Authorization only makes sense after authentication: first the system knows WHO, then it decides WHAT that identity may do.

blocks.label: Think first: Nikos logs in successfully but gets an error when running DELETE. Authentication or authorization problem?
blocks.text: **Authorization.** Login worked, so his identity was proven; the system simply doesn't allow that identity to delete.

sections.title: Principals: User, Group, Service Principal
sections.hook: Every grant goes TO a principal — pick the right kind and half of your security problems disappear.

blocks.text: A **principal** is an identity to which permissions can be given. Unity Catalog grants privileges to principals on securable objects.

items.def: A set of principals, e.g. `data_engineers` = Nikos, Maria, John.
A machine identity for automation, e.g. `orders-etl-prod`.

blocks.caption: Grant to groups, not individuals

blocks.title: Groups over individuals
blocks.text: Databricks recommends managing access through **groups** instead of individual users wherever possible. Then onboarding/offboarding = changing group membership.
A production job runs **every night at 02:00**. Ideally it should **not** 'run as Nikos'. What if Nikos leaves the company and his account is disabled? The job breaks.

human       ──►  user identity       (nikos@company.com)
automation  ──►  service principal   (orders-etl-prod)
blocks.caption: Humans use users; automation uses service principals

blocks.title: Why service principals for production?
blocks.text: A production workload needs a **stable machine identity** independent of the lifecycle and permissions of one specific employee. We'll use this again with Jobs and CI/CD.

sections.title: Securable Objects, Privileges & GRANT Grammar
sections.hook: Read GRANT like a sentence: give WHAT right, ON which object, TO whom.

blocks.text: A **securable object** is anything whose permissions you can control: catalog, schema, table, volume, function, …

blocks.code:
catalog:  company
schema:   company.finance
table:    company.finance.payroll
blocks.caption: Securables at three levels

blocks.text: A **privilege** is the action a principal is allowed to perform on a securable object.

head: Word
Meaning
blocks.caption: Parse it grammatically instead of memorizing it

blocks.text: To SELECT from `company.finance.transactions` you conceptually walk the path **company → finance → transactions**, so permissions usually include the containers too:

blocks.caption: The full path for a read

blocks.title: SELECT alone is not enough
blocks.text: Having SELECT on a table but **not USE CATALOG** (or USE SCHEMA) can still produce a permission problem: access passes through the catalog/schema hierarchy.

blocks.title: Coming later
blocks.text: Privilege inheritance and the exact Unity Catalog semantics come in the Unity Catalog chapter.

items.def: A governed object on which permissions can be granted (catalog, schema, table, volume, function…).
An action a principal may perform on a securable (SELECT, USE CATALOG, USE SCHEMA…).

sections.title: Debugging PERMISSION_DENIED
sections.hook: 'Give me admin' is not debugging. Walk the path — and check WHO is really running.

items.title: Bad debugging
points: Fixes the symptom, breaks least privilege
You learn nothing about the cause

items.title: Good debugging
points: Walk the access path step by step
Check the identity that actually runs

blocks.caption: The permission-debugging chain

blocks.title: The last question is the critical one
blocks.text: **You** may have SELECT. But the Job may run as `orders-prod-service-principal` — and that identity may not.

blocks.title: Ask yourself when you see PERMISSION_DENIED
questions: Can this principal access the workspace at all?
Does it have USE CATALOG on the catalog (prod)?
Does it have USE SCHEMA on the schema (finance)?
Does it have SELECT on the table itself?
Are row filters, column masks or other policies limiting it?
Which identity is ACTUALLY running this — me, or a job's service principal?

blocks.title: 'It works for me' proves nothing
blocks.text: Your own successful query only proves YOUR identity has the privileges. Always check the run identity of the job.

sections.title: Least Privilege
sections.hook: Give exactly what's needed — because every extra privilege is an extra way to break production.

blocks.text: **Least privilege**: give only the permissions that are necessary.
If an analyst needs `SELECT`, you do **not** give `ALL PRIVILEGES` 'so they can work more easily'.

blocks.title: Powerful privileges
blocks.text: Databricks specifically warns to use powerful privileges such as **ALL PRIVILEGES**, **MANAGE** and **ownership** sparingly.

items: Increases the **blast radius** (how much damage one mistake or compromised identity can do)
Risk of accidental or destructive actions

items.def: How much can be damaged if one identity makes a mistake or is compromised.

blocks.title: 'Give ALL PRIVILEGES to everybody'
blocks.text: It makes the error disappear today and creates a much bigger incident tomorrow.

blocks.label: Think first: an analyst needs to read gold.daily_sales. What exactly do they need?
blocks.text: USE CATALOG on the catalog, USE SCHEMA on the schema, SELECT on the table — nothing more (no MODIFY, no ALL PRIVILEGES, no ownership).

sections.title: Dev → Test/Staging → Prod
sections.hook: Never debug on the CEO's dashboard. Environments let you break things safely.

blocks.text: You have `prod.gold.monthly_revenue` feeding the **CEO dashboard**. You want to try `.filter(col("country") != "GR")` for debugging. Do you edit the production notebook and press **Run All**? **No.** You want **environment isolation**.

questions: Which version is running?
Who changed it?
When?

blocks.title: Manual production edits
blocks.text: You lose reproducibility, controlled review/testing, reliable version history and repeatable deployment.

sections.title: Source Control with Git
sections.hook: The source of truth is the repository — not 'that notebook Nikos has in his workspace'.

blocks.caption: Typical Git flow

blocks.text: The **source of truth** for code becomes the **Git repository** — not *"that notebook Nikos has in the workspace"*.

items.def: An isolated line of work for one change.
A recorded snapshot of changes with author and time.
A request to merge a branch, where the change is reviewed (and tested).
The shared branch that represents accepted code.

blocks.title: What Git gives you
blocks.text: Version history, who/what/when for every change, review before merge, and an easy way back to previous versions — the answers to the 'manual edit' questions.

blocks.label: Think first: which of the six 'manual edit' questions does Git answer?
blocks.text: Which version, who, when, what changed and how to go back. 'Did it pass tests?' needs CI on top of Git.

sections.title: CI and CD
sections.hook: Machines check every change (CI) and ship validated changes the same way every time (CD).

blocks.text: **CI — Continuous Integration.** You `git push`; the system automatically runs:

blocks.caption: A CI pipeline

blocks.title: CI gate
blocks.text: If anything fails: **don't merge / don't deploy.**
**CD** can mean **Continuous Delivery** or **Continuous Deployment** depending on the process. The core idea: validated artifact/code → automated, controlled deployment → target environment.

blocks.caption: A CD pipeline

items.title: CI
points: Automatic integration / validation / testing of code changes

blocks.title: Two meanings of CD
blocks.text: Continuous **Delivery** (ready to deploy, often with an approval) vs Continuous **Deployment** (deployed automatically). Either way: validated code → automated, controlled deployment.

sections.title: Infrastructure as Code & Declarative Automation Bundles
sections.hook: If a Job exists only as UI clicks, nobody can review it, version it or recreate it.

blocks.text: A Job needs: task A, task B, schedule, compute, parameters, permissions. You *can* create all of it manually in the UI — but in production it's often better to **declare it as code/configuration**.

blocks.code:
job:
  name: orders_pipeline
  schedule:
    ...
  tasks:
    - ingest
    - transform
blocks.caption: Conceptual job definition (not real syntax yet)

blocks.text: This is the philosophy of **Infrastructure as Code / configuration as code**.

blocks.title: Naming: Declarative Automation Bundles = Databricks Asset Bundles
blocks.text: The tool you'll learn later is called **Declarative Automation Bundles**; it was formerly called **Databricks Asset Bundles**. Tutorials saying 'Asset Bundles' mean the same concept.

Databricks recommends bundles as the main approach for CI/CD and IaC-style deployment of Databricks projects. A bundle can describe **jobs, pipelines, source files, tests and target environments**. The central file is usually **`databricks.yml`**.

blocks.code:
targets:
  dev:
    mode: development
  prod:
    mode: production
blocks.caption: databricks.yml targets with the two deployment modes

blocks.title: Don't memorize yet
blocks.text: We'll learn bundle syntax line by line in the Bundles chapter. For now: bundle = project + resources + targets, as code.

sections.title: Debugging Case 1: No New Data Appears
sections.hook: Source has today's data, Gold doesn't. Walk the pipeline — don't blame the platform.

blocks.text: Pipeline: **source files → bronze → silver → gold**. The source has today's data. **Gold doesn't.**

blocks.title: Don't say 'Databricks bug'
blocks.text: Think in pipeline terms and check each layer in order.

blocks.caption: The layer-by-layer check

blocks.title: Ask yourself when new data doesn't show up
questions: Source: do the new files/events really exist?
Bronze: were they ingested?
Checkpoint: did it advance?
Silver: did the transformation reject (filter/quarantine) the rows?
Schema: did it change and block the write?
CDC: are sequence and key correct?
Gold: did the refresh/job actually run?

blocks.title: The golden rule of this course
blocks.text: **Find the first layer at which reality diverges from what you expected.** Everything upstream of it is fine; the bug lives at that boundary.

blocks.label: Think first (test Q25): Kafka → Bronze → Silver → Gold. Kafka has event 500. Bronze has event 500. Silver doesn't. Where do you start?
blocks.text: At the **Bronze → Silver boundary** — you've already proven the event reached Bronze, so source and ingestion are fine.

sections.title: Debugging Case 2: Duplicate Records
sections.hook: 'I have duplicates' is a symptom, not a root cause — there are at least seven very different causes.

blocks.caption: The symptom

head: Possible cause
Where it lives / what to check
rows: Source: does the source itself contain order 123 twice?
Source → Bronze: was the same file loaded twice?
Job: did a retry re-write data that was already written?
Silver: is the key really unique per entity?
Silver: is there a dedup step at all?
Silver/Gold: does the MERGE ON clause match existing rows?
blocks.caption: Seven very different root causes

blocks.title: Symptom ≠ root cause
blocks.text: "I have duplicates" is **not** a root cause. It's a symptom. Your job is to find which mechanism created the second copy.

blocks.title: Ask yourself when you see duplicate records
questions: Does the source itself contain the duplicate?
Was the same file/batch ingested twice into Bronze?
Was a streaming checkpoint reset or moved?
Did a job retry re-write data it had already written?
Is the CDC/business key I use really unique?
Does my Silver logic deduplicate at all?
Is my MERGE condition matching on the right key?

blocks.code:
-- BUG: matching on a changing column means updates never match
MERGE INTO silver.orders t
USING updates s
ON t.order_id = s.order_id AND t.updated_at = s.updated_at
WHEN MATCHED THEN UPDATE SET *
WHEN NOT MATCHED THEN INSERT *;
blocks.caption: An incorrect MERGE condition that inserts a second order 123

blocks.title: Deduplicating blindly
blocks.text: Adding `DISTINCT` everywhere may hide the symptom while the real cause (e.g. a reset checkpoint or wrong MERGE key) keeps producing bad data.

sections.title: Debugging Case 3: Works in Dev, Fails in Prod
sections.hook: Perfect code can still fail — because prod is a different execution environment.

blocks.text: The code may be perfect. What can differ between environments:

head: Group
What may differ
blocks.caption: Nine differences, grouped WHO → WHAT → HOW → WHERE

blocks.title: Not just the traceback
blocks.text: Production debugging isn't just reading the Python traceback. You must understand the **whole execution environment**.

blocks.title: Works when I run it, fails when scheduled (test Q26)
blocks.text: One of the first things to check: the **run identity**. You may have the permissions while the scheduled execution identity does not.

blocks.title: Ask yourself when it works in dev but fails in prod
questions: Which identity runs it in prod — and is it the same one that ran it in dev?
Does that identity have the needed permissions in prod?
Am I pointing at the right catalog and schema for prod (not dev_…)?
Does prod use a storage credential this identity can use?
Is the prod configuration (parameters, paths) different?
Do the secrets exist in prod and can this identity read them?
Is the compute different (type, access mode, size)?
Is the runtime version different?

blocks.title: Assuming the code is the problem
blocks.text: When only the environment changed, the code is the least likely suspect. Compare environments before rewriting code.

blocks.text: Find the **first layer where reality diverges** from what you expected. Symptoms (missing data, duplicates, PERMISSION_DENIED) are not root causes.

askYourself: Can this principal access the workspace at all?
Does it have USE CATALOG on prod?

steps.do: Identify the executing identity (user vs job run-as / service principal)
steps.why: Your privileges don't transfer to other identities.

steps.do: Check the privilege path for that identity
Check fine-grained policies (row filters / masks)
steps.why: They can restrict even with SELECT.

steps.do: Grant only the missing privilege, ideally to a group or the service principal

rootCauses: Job runs as a different identity without grants
debug.fix: Grant exactly the missing privilege to the identity that actually runs the workload.
debug.mnemonic: Workspace → Catalog → Schema → Table → Policies → WHO? (W-C-S-T-P-Who)

debug.title: No new data appears in Gold
debug.symptom: The source has today's data, but Gold doesn't.
askYourself: Source: do the new files/events really exist?
Bronze: were they ingested?
Checkpoint: did it advance?
Silver: did the transformation reject the rows?
Schema: did it change?
CDC: are sequence and key correct?
Gold: did the refresh/job run?

steps.do: Confirm new data at the source
Count today's rows in Bronze
steps.why: Splits ingestion problems from transformation problems.

steps.do: Inspect the stream checkpoint progress
steps.why: A stuck checkpoint means nothing new is read.

steps.do: Look for rejected/quarantined rows and schema errors in Silver
steps.why: Validation or schema mismatch can drop the rows.

steps.do: Verify CDC sequence/key logic
steps.why: Wrong ordering or keys can hide changes.

steps.do: Check the Gold job/refresh run history

debug.fix: Fix the first layer where reality diverges, then let the downstream layers catch up (or rerun them).
debug.mnemonic: Source · Bronze · Checkpoint · Silver · Schema · CDC · Gold — 'Some Big Cats Sleep Soundly Chasing Geese'

debug.title: Duplicate records
debug.symptom: The same record appears twice (e.g. order 123 twice) in Silver or Gold.
askYourself: Does the source itself contain the duplicate?
Was the same file ingested twice?
Was a checkpoint reset?
Did a retry re-write data already written?
Is the CDC key correct and unique?
Is deduplication missing?
Is the MERGE condition correct?

steps.do: Find the first layer where the duplicate appears (source, Bronze, Silver)
For Bronze duplicates: check ingestion history and checkpoint
Check job run history for retries
steps.why: Non-idempotent writes duplicate data on retry.

steps.do: Review CDC key, dedup step and MERGE ON clause
steps.code:
MERGE INTO silver.orders t
USING updates s
ON t.order_id = s.order_id
...

debug.fix: Fix the mechanism that created the second copy, then clean existing duplicates (e.g. dedup in Silver). Never just hide them with DISTINCT.
debug.mnemonic: 'Some Files Can Repeat; Keys, Dedup, MERGE' (S-F-C-R-K-D-M)

debug.title: Works in dev, fails in prod
debug.symptom: DEV: success. PROD: PERMISSION_DENIED (or another failure) with identical code.
askYourself: Which identity runs it in prod, and is it the same as in dev?
Does that identity have the needed permissions in prod?
Am I using the right prod catalog?
Am I using the right prod schema?
Is there a storage credential this identity can use?
Is the prod configuration different?
Do the needed secrets exist in prod?
Is the compute different?
Is the runtime different?

steps.do: Compare run identity between dev and prod
Check privileges and object names in prod
steps.why: Catalog/schema names and grants differ per environment.

steps.do: Diff configuration and secrets between targets
Compare compute type and runtime version

debug.fix: Make environments differ only in deliberate, declared ways (bundle targets), and grant the prod identity exactly what it needs.
debug.mnemonic: WHO → WHAT → HOW → WHERE (identity → permissions/catalog/schema/credential → config/secret → compute/runtime)

debug.title: Works when I run it, fails when scheduled
debug.symptom: A pipeline succeeds when run manually but fails when the scheduled job runs it.
askYourself: Which identity does the scheduled run use?
Is it the same identity as my manual run?
Does the scheduled identity have USE CATALOG, USE SCHEMA and SELECT/MODIFY where needed?
Does it differ in configuration, secrets or compute from my manual run?

steps.do: Open the job settings and read the run-as identity
steps.why: Manual runs use you; scheduled runs may not.

steps.do: Check that identity's grants along the path
Grant the minimal privilege and re-run

debug.fix: Check run identity first; grant the scheduled identity exactly what it needs.

debug.title: Nobody knows what is running in production
debug.symptom: Prod output changed overnight; someone edited the production notebook manually and pressed Run All.
askYourself: Which version is running?
Who changed it?
When?
What changed?
How do I return to the previous version?
Did this same code pass tests?

steps.do: Try to reconstruct the change from notebook history / colleagues
Restore known-good code
Move the code into Git with review, CI and CD via bundles
steps.why: Make the six questions answerable next time.

debug.fix: Dev → staging → prod with Git, CI and CD (bundles). Never edit production by hand.
debug.mnemonic: Which · Who · When · What · Way back · Tested? (6 Ws)

exercises.q: Test Q14: What is the difference between authentication and authorization?
exercises.model: Authentication answers 'who are you?' — it proves an identity, e.g. that the login really is nikos@company.com. Authorization answers 'what are you allowed to do?' — e.g. Nikos may SELECT customers but not DELETE or CREATE TABLE.
rubric: authentication = who are you / prove identity
authorization = what are you allowed to do
exercises.explain: Official answer: Authentication — who are you? Authorization — what are you allowed to do?

exercises.q: Authentication or authorization?

items.text: Checking whether Nikos may DELETE customers
Proving the caller really is the service principal orders-etl-prod
GRANT SELECT ON TABLE ... TO analysts
A login fails because of a wrong password/token
PERMISSION_DENIED on a SELECT after a successful login

exercises.explain: Authentication = establishing identity (login, token). Authorization = permissions of that identity (grants, PERMISSION_DENIED).

exercises.q: PERMISSION_DENIED after you have successfully logged in is an authentication problem.
exercises.explain: You are already authenticated (the system knows who you are). PERMISSION_DENIED means that identity lacks a privilege — an authorization problem.

exercises.q: Complete the two questions.
exercises.text: Authentication asks: [[who are you|who are you?]] — Authorization asks: [[what are you allowed to do|what are you allowed to do?|what may you do]]
exercises.explain: Two separate checks: identity first, then permissions for that identity.

exercises.q: Which one is NOT an authorization decision?
options: Nikos proves his identity at login

exercises.model: An identity to which privileges can be assigned — for example a user, a group or a service principal.
rubric: privileges/permissions can be granted to it
exercises.explain: Official answer: an identity to which privileges can be assigned, e.g. user, group or service principal.

exercises.q: Test Q16: Why should a production job usually run as a service principal instead of a developer's personal account?
options: Production needs a stable machine identity independent of one employee's lifecycle and permissions
Personal accounts cannot run jobs on a schedule
Service principals automatically get ALL PRIVILEGES
why: They can — that's exactly the risk.
No! Service principals should also follow least privilege.
exercises.explain: If the job runs as Nikos and Nikos leaves (account disabled) or his permissions change, production breaks. A service principal like `orders-etl-prod` is owned by the system, not a person.

exercises.q: Match each example to its principal type.
exercises.explain: Users = humans, groups = sets of principals, service principals = machine identities for automation.

exercises.q: Which one is NOT a principal?
exercises.explain: `company.finance.payroll` is a table — a securable object you grant ON. The other three are identities you grant TO.

exercises.q: The nightly `orders` job has run fine for a year. Today it fails at 02:00. Yesterday Nikos — the engineer who created it — left the company.

steps.prompt: What is your first hypothesis?

options.text: The job runs as Nikos's user identity, which was just disabled
options.fb: Right — a classic reason to use service principals for production.

options.text: The data volume suddenly grew
options.fb: Possible in general, but the timing with Nikos leaving is the strong clue.

options.text: Spark has a bug
options.fb: Don't blame the platform before checking the identity.

steps.prompt: Confirmed: 'Run as' = nikos@company.com. What is the durable fix?

options.text: Run the job as a service principal (e.g. orders-etl-prod) with only the privileges it needs
options.fb: Stable machine identity + least privilege.

options.text: Run it as another engineer's account
options.fb: Same problem again when that person leaves or changes role.

options.text: Re-enable Nikos's account forever
options.fb: Keeps a departed employee's identity alive — a security risk.

exercises.explain: Human → user identity; automation → service principal.

exercises.q: Grant the group `data_engineers` SELECT on table `company.silver.orders` (one statement).
exercises.solution: GRANT SELECT ON TABLE company.silver.orders TO `data_engineers`;
exercises.explain: Granting to a group means you manage access by membership; backticks are used around principal names in Databricks SQL.

exercises.q: Nikos, Maria and John each need the same 4 privileges. How many GRANT statements do you write if you grant per user (instead of 4 grants to `data_engineers`)?
exercises.explain: 3 users × 4 privileges = 12 statements, versus 4 when granting to the group — and with the group, onboarding a 4th engineer needs 0 new grants, just a membership change.

exercises.q: Databricks recommends granting privileges to individual users rather than groups wherever possible.
exercises.explain: The recommendation is the opposite: manage access through groups where possible, and manage membership.

exercises.q: Test Q17: What is a securable object?
exercises.model: A governed object on which permissions can be granted — e.g. a catalog, schema, table, volume or function.
rubric: permissions can be granted on it
exercises.explain: Official answer: a governed object on which permissions can be granted.

exercises.q: Test Q18: Explain `GRANT SELECT ON TABLE prod.finance.transactions TO analysts;` word by word — match each part to its meaning.
exercises.explain: GRANT = give, SELECT = privilege, ON TABLE … = securable, TO … = principal. Reading it as a sentence prevents mechanical memorization.

exercises.q: Test Q19: A group has SELECT on a table but NOT USE CATALOG on its catalog. Can there be a permission problem?
options: No — SELECT on the table is all you need
Yes — access passes through the catalog/schema hierarchy
Only if the table is a view
exercises.explain: To reach `catalog.schema.table` the principal also needs USE CATALOG on the catalog and USE SCHEMA on the schema. Missing either blocks the read.

exercises.q: Write the three GRANT statements that let group `analysts` read `company.finance.transactions`.
exercises.explain: Walk the path: catalog → schema → table. Each level needs its own privilege.

exercises.q: A brand-new group has no privileges at all. What is the minimum number of GRANT statements so it can SELECT from one table `prod.finance.transactions` (as taught in the lesson)?
exercises.explain: USE CATALOG on prod, USE SCHEMA on prod.finance, SELECT on the table — one per level of the three-level name.

exercises.q: Order the grants along the access path (outer container first).
exercises.explain: The path goes company → finance → transactions; the outer containers must be usable before the table can be read.

exercises.q: Principal, securable object or privilege?
exercises.explain: Principal = WHO (TO …); securable = WHAT object (ON …); privilege = WHICH action (GRANT …).

exercises.q: This script should let `analysts` read `company.finance.transactions`. Click the buggy lines.
lines: GRANT USE CATALOG ON CATALOG company TO `analysts`;
GRANT USE SCHEMA ON TABLE company.finance TO `analysts`;
GRANT SELECT ON TABLE company.finance TO `analysts`;
exercises.fix:
GRANT USE SCHEMA ON SCHEMA company.finance TO `analysts`;
GRANT SELECT ON TABLE company.finance.transactions TO `analysts`;
exercises.explain: USE SCHEMA is granted ON SCHEMA (not ON TABLE), and SELECT needs the full three-level table name — `company.finance` is a schema, not a table.

exercises.q: Order the PERMISSION_DENIED checks exactly as taught.
items: Can the principal access the workspace?
Does it have SELECT on the table?
Are there row filters / masks / policies?
exercises.explain: Walk from the outside in (workspace → catalog → schema → table → fine-grained policies), and never forget the run identity, which is often the real cause.

exercises.q: If my own SELECT on a table works, a scheduled job that reads the same table cannot get PERMISSION_DENIED.
exercises.explain: The job may run as a different identity (e.g. a service principal) with different privileges. 'Which identity is actually running?' is the critical check.

exercises.q: `SELECT * FROM prod.finance.transactions` works in your notebook, but the nightly Job fails with `PERMISSION_DENIED`.

steps.prompt: What do you check first?

options.text: Which identity the Job actually runs as
options.fb: Your success proves only your privileges; the job's identity is the prime suspect.

options.text: Ask an admin for ALL PRIVILEGES on prod
options.fb: That's the 'give me admin' anti-pattern.

options.text: Rewrite the query in Python
options.fb: Language doesn't change permissions.

steps.prompt: It runs as `orders-prod-service-principal`. Which privileges must you verify for it?

options.text: USE CATALOG on prod, USE SCHEMA on prod.finance, SELECT on the table (plus any row filters/masks)
options.fb: That's the full path for a read.

options.text: Only SELECT on the table
options.fb: Without USE CATALOG / USE SCHEMA the read still fails.

options.text: MANAGE on the catalog
options.fb: Far more than needed — violates least privilege.

steps.prompt: It lacks USE SCHEMA on prod.finance. Fix?

options.text: GRANT USE SCHEMA ON SCHEMA prod.finance TO the service principal
options.fb: Grant exactly the missing privilege.

options.text: Make the service principal a workspace admin
options.fb: Huge blast radius for a one-privilege problem.

options.text: Run the job as your own user
options.fb: Ties production to a person — the exact thing service principals avoid.

exercises.explain: Path + identity: workspace → catalog → schema → table → policies → who is ACTUALLY running.

exercises.q: Complete the permission-debugging chain.
exercises.text: workspace access → USE [[CATALOG]] → USE [[SCHEMA]] → [[SELECT]] on table → row filters / masks / policies → which [[identity]] is ACTUALLY running?
exercises.explain: Outer containers first, then the table, then fine-grained policies, and finally the run identity — the check that most often explains 'works for me, fails in the job'.

exercises.q: Which response to PERMISSION_DENIED is the 'bad debugging' the lesson warns about?
options: Checking USE CATALOG on the catalog
Checking which identity runs the job
Asking for admin rights so it 'just works'
exercises.explain: Requesting admin hides the cause and breaks least privilege. The other three are steps of the correct debugging chain.

exercises.q: Explain why 'Which identity is ACTUALLY running?' is the most important PERMISSION_DENIED question.
exercises.model: Because permissions belong to identities. When I test interactively my user identity runs the query, but a scheduled job usually runs as another identity, often a service principal like orders-prod-service-principal. My grants don't apply to it, so the job can fail even though the same query works for me.
rubric: interactive = my user; job = service principal / run-as
exercises.explain: This single check explains most 'works for me, fails in the job' permission incidents.

exercises.q: Which is NOT part of the PERMISSION_DENIED checklist?
exercises.explain: Shuffle partitions affect performance, never permissions. The other three are steps of the permission chain.

exercises.q: Test Q20: Why is 'give ALL PRIVILEGES to everybody' a bad solution to permission errors?
exercises.model: It violates least privilege, increases the blast radius, raises the risk of accidental or destructive actions, and increases security exposure. It also hides the real missing privilege instead of fixing it.
exercises.explain: Official answer: violates least privilege, increases blast radius, risk of accidental/destructive actions and security exposure.

exercises.q: An analyst only needs to read one table. Which grant set follows least privilege?
options: USE CATALOG + USE SCHEMA + SELECT on the table
exercises.explain: Grant exactly the read path. ALL PRIVILEGES, MANAGE and ownership are powerful privileges Databricks says to use sparingly.

exercises.q: Select ALL the consequences of over-granting privileges.
exercises.explain: Over-granting has only downsides for safety; privileges don't change performance.

exercises.q: ALL PRIVILEGES, MANAGE and ownership should be used sparingly.
exercises.explain: Databricks explicitly warns about these powerful privileges; they should be reserved for the few identities that truly administer objects.

exercises.q: Which grant does NOT fit 'least privilege for a read-only analyst'?
exercises.explain: ALL PRIVILEGES includes writes and more — far beyond read-only needs.

exercises.q: Test Q21: Why shouldn't you edit a production notebook manually?
exercises.model: Because you lose reproducibility, controlled review and testing, reliable version history and repeatable deployment. Afterwards nobody can reliably say which version runs, who changed what and when, how to roll back, or whether that code passed tests.
exercises.explain: Official answer: you lose reproducibility, controlled review/testing, reliable version history and repeatable deployment.

exercises.q: Which environment is this typical of?

items.text: Validating permissions, dependencies and configuration before release
Integration and data-quality checks without affecting real consumers
It's fine to break things here

exercises.explain: DEV = freedom to break; STAGING = production-like validation without real consumers; PROD = controlled, monitored, restricted.

exercises.q: Order the path a code change should take.
exercises.explain: Changes are developed in DEV, validated in a production-like STAGING environment, and only then reach PROD.

exercises.q: Test/staging is where you validate permissions, dependencies, configuration, integration, data quality and deployment without affecting real consumers.
exercises.explain: That is exactly the role of staging: be close to prod, but isolated from real consumers.

exercises.q: The CEO's monthly revenue numbers changed overnight. A colleague says: 'I just tested a filter in the prod notebook and pressed Run All.'

steps.prompt: What's the first problem you face?

options.text: You can't reliably tell which version ran, what changed, or how to roll back
options.fb: Manual edits leave no reliable version history or review trail.

options.text: The cluster is too small
options.fb: Compute size is not the issue here.

options.text: Unity Catalog is down
options.fb: Nothing points to governance.

steps.prompt: What should the process have been?

options.text: Change code in DEV, commit to Git, review, test in STAGING, deploy to PROD automatically
options.fb: Environment isolation + source control + CI/CD.

options.text: Edit prod but warn the CEO first
options.fb: Still no review, tests or reproducibility.

options.text: Copy the prod notebook and edit the copy in prod
options.fb: Still running untested code against prod data.

exercises.explain: Production changes must be reproducible, reviewed, tested and reversible.

exercises.q: A manual prod edit broke a dashboard. Order the questions you'd need answered (the lesson's list).
items: How do I return to the previous version?
Did the same code pass tests?
exercises.explain: These six questions are exactly what Git + CI/CD answer reliably — and what manual edits make unanswerable.

exercises.q: Order the Git flow.
exercises.explain: Work happens on a branch, is recorded in commits, proposed via a pull request, reviewed, and only then merged into main.

exercises.q: What is the source of truth for production code in a mature setup?
exercises.explain: Code lives and is versioned in Git; workspaces get their code from it. A personal workspace notebook has no reliable history or review.

exercises.q: Match each Git term to its role.
pairs: isolated line of work for a change
proposal to merge, where review happens
exercises.explain: Together these give versioning, traceability and review before code reaches production.

exercises.q: Using Git alone already guarantees that the code passed tests.
exercises.explain: Git gives history and review. Automatic testing of each change is CI (Continuous Integration), built on top of Git.

exercises.q: Test Q22: What is CI?
exercises.model: Automatic integration, validation and testing of code changes — e.g. lint, unit tests, integration tests, configuration validation and build on every push; if anything fails, you don't merge or deploy.
rubric: integration / validation / testing of code changes
exercises.explain: Official answer: automatic integration/validation/testing of code changes.

exercises.q: Test Q23: What is CD?
exercises.model: Controlled delivery or deployment of validated changes to the target environments, e.g. main → tests → deploy staging → integration tests → deploy production.
exercises.explain: Official answer: controlled delivery/deployment of the validated changes to the target environments.

exercises.q: Order the CI pipeline from the lesson.
exercises.explain: Cheap, fast checks first (lint, unit tests), slower ones later (integration, config validation), and build at the end.

exercises.q: Order the CD pipeline from the lesson.
exercises.explain: Validated code moves to staging, is integration-tested there, and only then is deployed to production.

exercises.q: CI fails on the integration tests for your pull request. What should happen?
options: Merge anyway and fix in prod
Deploy to prod but not staging
exercises.explain: CI is a gate: a failing check blocks merge and deploy. Disabling tests or 'fixing in prod' defeats its purpose.

exercises.q: CD always means fully automatic deployment to production with no human approval.
exercises.explain: CD can mean Continuous Delivery or Continuous Deployment depending on the process; the shared idea is automated, controlled deployment of validated code.

exercises.q: CI or CD?

items.text: Run lint and unit tests on every push
Deploy to staging after merge to main
Promote the validated version to production

exercises.explain: CI validates the change; CD ships the validated change to environments.

exercises.q: Test Q24: What do we gain when a Job's definition lives in YAML/Git instead of only UI clicks? Select ALL that apply.
exercises.explain: Official answer: version control, review, reproducibility, automation, repeatable deployments, environment-specific configuration. Configuration as code doesn't make Spark itself faster.

exercises.q: 'Databricks Asset Bundles' and 'Declarative Automation Bundles' are two completely different concepts.
exercises.explain: Declarative Automation Bundles is the current name; Databricks Asset Bundles was the earlier name of the same tool.

exercises.q: Complete the bundle targets in `databricks.yml`.
exercises.explain: Databricks explicitly supports `development` and `production` deployment modes for bundle targets.

exercises.q: Write the `targets` section of a `databricks.yml` with a `dev` target in development mode and a `prod` target in production mode.
exercises.solution:
targets:
  dev:
    mode: development
  prod:
    mode: production
exercises.explain: Targets are the environments a bundle deploys to; each declares its mode. Exact further syntax comes in the Bundles chapter.

exercises.q: A teammate summarized bundles. Click the WRONG statements.
lines: A bundle can describe jobs, pipelines, source files, tests and target environments.
The central configuration file is usually databricks.yml.
Bundles are a different technology from the old Databricks Asset Bundles.
Targets can use the modes development and production.
Bundles are meant only for one-off manual deployments from the UI.
exercises.fix:
Declarative Automation Bundles are the renamed Databricks Asset Bundles (same concept).
Bundles are the recommended basis for CI/CD and IaC-style, automated, repeatable deployments.
exercises.explain: Bundles = renamed Asset Bundles, designed for automated CI/CD deployment — the opposite of manual UI clicks.

exercises.q: Explain Infrastructure as Code to a teammate who builds all Jobs by clicking in the UI.
exercises.model: Instead of creating the job's tasks, schedule, compute, parameters and permissions by hand, you declare them in a configuration file (e.g. YAML in a bundle). That file lives in Git, gets reviewed, has version history, can recreate the same job anywhere, and can be deployed automatically to dev, staging and prod by CI/CD.
exercises.explain: The point isn't YAML itself — it's that configuration gets the same safety net as code.

exercises.q: Match each platform concern to what handles it.
pairs: Delta tables on cloud object storage
exercises.explain: Keeping these five concerns separate is what makes debugging possible: each failure usually lives in one of them.

exercises.q: Which name is NOT a (past or present) name for Databricks' declarative pipeline product?
exercises.explain: Bundles are the deployment/IaC tool (formerly Asset Bundles). The other three are names along the DLT → Lakeflow pipelines evolution.

exercises.q: According to current docs, what do Lakeflow pipelines build on?
exercises.explain: Lakeflow pipelines build on Apache Spark Declarative Pipelines and support batch + streaming in SQL/Python with automatic dependency orchestration and incremental processing.

exercises.q: Which capabilities does the lesson attribute to Lakeflow pipelines? Select ALL.
exercises.explain: Governance (grants) is Unity Catalog's job, not the pipeline engine's.

exercises.q: A tutorial about 'Delta Live Tables' is about a totally unrelated product from Lakeflow pipelines.
exercises.explain: DLT is an older name in the same lineage: DLT → Lakeflow Declarative Pipelines → Lakeflow pipelines on Spark Declarative Pipelines.

exercises.q: Which layer of the platform does each item belong to?

items.text: Delta tables on cloud object storage

exercises.explain: Execution computes, governance controls access, deployment ships code/config, storage keeps the data.

exercises.q: Order the 'no new data' checks exactly as taught.
items: Source: do the new files exist?
exercises.explain: Follow the data from source to Gold. The first check that fails is the layer where reality diverges — that's where the bug lives.

exercises.q: Test Q25: Kafka has event 500, Bronze has event 500, Silver does not. Where do you start debugging?
why: Kafka has the event — the producer is fine.
Bronze has the event — ingestion is fine.
Correct: first layer where reality diverges.
Gold is downstream of the problem.
exercises.explain: The event is proven to be in Bronze, so everything up to Bronze works. The first divergence is Bronze → Silver (validation, schema, CDC, dedup, filters).

exercises.q: Source has today's files; Gold shows nothing for today.

steps.prompt: Where do you start?

options.text: At the source: confirm the new files really exist
options.fb: Start at the beginning and walk forward.

options.text: Open a ticket: Databricks bug
options.fb: Never the first hypothesis.

options.text: Rebuild Gold from scratch
options.fb: You don't know yet where data stops.

steps.prompt: Files exist, but Bronze has no rows for today. What next?

options.text: Check whether ingestion ran and whether the checkpoint advanced
options.fb: Data stops at Source → Bronze: ingestion + checkpoint are the suspects.

options.text: Check Silver's dedup logic
options.fb: Silver can't process rows Bronze never received.

options.text: Check Gold refresh
options.fb: Too far downstream.

steps.prompt: Alternate timeline: Bronze AND Silver have today's rows, Gold doesn't. Suspect?

options.text: Gold refresh/job didn't run (or its aggregation filtered the rows)
options.fb: First divergence is Silver → Gold.

options.text: The checkpoint
options.fb: Ingestion is proven fine — Bronze and Silver have the data.

options.text: Schema at source
options.fb: Rows already flowed through Silver.

exercises.explain: Find the first layer where reality diverges from expectation.

exercises.q: Bronze has today's rows; Silver doesn't. The Silver job ran successfully.

steps.prompt: Which group of causes lives at the Bronze → Silver boundary?

options.text: Rows rejected by validation, a schema change, wrong CDC sequence/key
options.fb: These are exactly the Silver, Schema and CDC checks.

options.text: Source files missing
options.fb: Bronze already has them.

options.text: Gold refresh schedule
options.fb: Gold is after Silver.

steps.prompt: You find a new quarantine table full of today's rows with 'amount is not DECIMAL'. Meaning?

options.text: The Silver transformation rejected them — investigate the schema/type change upstream
options.fb: Rejected rows + type complaint → follow the schema-mismatch decision tree.

options.text: Delete the quarantine table and rerun
options.fb: That hides the evidence and loses data.

options.text: The checkpoint is broken
options.fb: Rows were ingested — the checkpoint did its job.

exercises.explain: 'Silver: rejected rows?' and 'Schema: changed?' are consecutive checks for a reason.

exercises.q: When Gold lacks today's data, the efficient approach is to start checking at Gold and work backwards randomly.
exercises.explain: Walk the pipeline systematically and find the FIRST layer where data diverges from expectation. Starting at the source (or bisecting with evidence like 'Bronze has event 500') prevents guessing.

exercises.q: State the course's general debugging principle and apply it to: 'Kafka has event 500, Bronze has it, Silver doesn't'.
exercises.model: Find the first layer at which reality diverges from what you expected. Kafka and Bronze both have event 500, so source and ingestion work; Silver doesn't, so the first divergence is Bronze → Silver — I investigate validation/rejected rows, schema changes and CDC key/sequence there.
exercises.explain: The principle turns a vague 'data is missing' into one specific boundary to inspect.

exercises.q: 'We have duplicates' is a root cause.
exercises.explain: It's a symptom. Causes range from the source producing duplicates to a wrong MERGE condition — each needs a different fix.

exercises.q: Complete the key sentence.
exercises.text: "I have duplicates" is not a [[root cause]]. It is a [[symptom]].
exercises.explain: Seven different mechanisms can produce the same duplicate symptom; each needs a different fix.

exercises.q: Which of these is NOT one of the seven duplicate causes listed in the lesson?
exercises.explain: Shuffle partition count affects performance, not row multiplicity. The listed causes: source duplicate, file ingested twice, checkpoint reset, retry semantics, CDC key incorrect, dedup missing, MERGE condition incorrect.

exercises.q: Where does each duplicate cause live?
exercises.explain: Locating the cause by layer tells you where to look first and which fix applies.

exercises.q: Silver `orders` contains order 123 twice.

steps.prompt: First question?

options.text: Does Bronze (the raw source data) already contain order 123 twice?
options.fb: This splits upstream causes from Silver-logic causes.

options.text: Add SELECT DISTINCT to Gold
options.fb: Hides the symptom without finding the mechanism.

options.text: Increase cluster size
options.fb: Duplicates aren't a capacity issue.

steps.prompt: Bronze has order 123 twice, from two different files with the same content. Next?

options.text: Check whether the same file was ingested twice or the checkpoint was reset
options.fb: Same content in two loads → ingestion/checkpoint suspects.

options.text: Check the Gold refresh
options.fb: Gold is downstream.

options.text: Check schema evolution
options.fb: Schema doesn't duplicate rows.

steps.prompt: Other timeline: Bronze has order 123 once (an insert) and once more as an update; Silver has 2 rows. Suspect?

options.text: The MERGE condition or CDC key is wrong, so the update was inserted instead of matched
options.fb: Update not matched → WHEN NOT MATCHED THEN INSERT → duplicate.

options.text: Source produced a duplicate
options.fb: The source sent an insert + an update, which is valid.

options.text: Checkpoint reset
options.fb: Bronze shows no replay.

exercises.explain: Duplicates are a symptom; trace them to the mechanism.

exercises.q: Order a sensible duplicate investigation (upstream first).
items: Does the source itself contain the duplicate?
Was the same file ingested twice into Bronze?
Was the checkpoint reset, or did a retry re-write data?
Is the CDC/business key correct and unique?
Does Silver deduplicate, and is the MERGE condition right?
exercises.explain: Upstream checks first: if Bronze already holds the duplicate, Silver logic isn't the origin (though missing dedup may fail to remove it).

exercises.q: This MERGE keeps creating a second row for order 123 whenever the order is updated. Click the buggy line.
lines: ON t.order_id = s.order_id AND t.updated_at = s.updated_at
exercises.explain: An update carries a new `updated_at`, so `t.updated_at = s.updated_at` never matches the existing row; it falls into WHEN NOT MATCHED and gets inserted again. Match on the business key only.

exercises.q: Your manager says: 'Just add DISTINCT and close the duplicates ticket.' Respond professionally.
exercises.model: Duplicates are a symptom, not a root cause. DISTINCT might hide them in one query but the mechanism — e.g. a file ingested twice, a reset checkpoint, a retry, a wrong CDC key or MERGE condition, or missing dedup — will keep producing bad data and affect other consumers. Let me first find where the second copy appears (source, Bronze, Silver) and fix that mechanism; then we add proper dedup in Silver if needed.
rubric: find where the duplicate first appears
exercises.explain: Good answers redirect from the symptom to the first layer where the duplicate appears.

exercises.q: Test Q26: A pipeline runs correctly when YOU run it but fails when it runs scheduled. One of the first things to check?
options: The run identity of the scheduled execution
The number of files in Bronze
exercises.explain: You may have the permissions, but the scheduled execution identity (often a service principal) may not. Identity is the classic difference between manual and scheduled runs.

exercises.q: Group the nine dev-vs-prod differences.
exercises.explain: WHO → WHAT → HOW → WHERE is a compact way to remember all nine items from the lesson.

exercises.q: A job works in DEV. In PROD it fails with `PERMISSION_DENIED`. The code is identical.

steps.prompt: What do you check first?

options.text: The identity running in prod vs dev
options.fb: WHO first — permissions belong to identities.

options.text: Rewrite the code
options.fb: Identical code succeeded in dev; the environment differs.

options.text: Upgrade the runtime
options.fb: PERMISSION_DENIED points at identity/permissions, not runtime.

steps.prompt: Prod runs as a service principal. What next?

options.text: Verify its privileges along the path in the PROD catalog/schema (and storage credential if it touches external storage)
options.fb: WHAT it may touch in prod.

options.text: Give it ALL PRIVILEGES
options.fb: Violates least privilege.

options.text: Switch prod to run as your user
options.fb: Ties production to a person.

steps.prompt: Privileges look right. The code reads a table name from a parameter. What else could differ?

options.text: Configuration: the prod parameter may point at a different catalog/schema (e.g. still dev_…)
options.fb: HOW it's configured — config, then secrets.

options.text: Shuffle partitions
options.fb: Performance setting, not a permission cause.

options.text: Nothing else can differ
options.fb: Config, secrets, compute and runtime can all differ.

exercises.explain: Dev and prod differ in identity, permissions, catalog, schema, storage credential, configuration, secret, compute and runtime.

exercises.q: Order the dev-vs-prod checks using the WHO → WHAT → HOW → WHERE grouping.
exercises.explain: Start with identity because it changes everything downstream; then what that identity may access; then configuration; finally the compute environment.

exercises.q: A notebook succeeds when you click Run, but the same notebook as a scheduled Job fails every night.

steps.prompt: What's one of the first things to check?

options.text: Under which identity the scheduled run executes
options.fb: Official answer: run identity.

options.text: Whether the notebook has too many cells
options.fb: Cell count isn't a failure cause.

options.text: Whether the schedule time is correct
options.fb: It runs — and fails — so scheduling works.

steps.prompt: The job runs as a service principal that lacks SELECT on one table. Fix?

options.text: Grant that specific privilege (and the USE CATALOG/USE SCHEMA path) to the service principal
options.fb: Least-privilege fix for the actual gap.

options.text: Change 'Run as' to your own user
options.fb: Works until you leave or your permissions change.

options.text: Give the service principal MANAGE on the catalog
options.fb: Far too broad.

exercises.explain: Manual vs scheduled differ mainly in identity.

exercises.q: Your notebook works manually but fails as a scheduled job. Order the checks.
items: Compare it with the identity used in the manual run
Check that identity's privileges along the catalog → schema → table path
exercises.explain: Identity first, then the privilege path, then a least-privilege fix, then verify.

exercises.q: If code works in dev, a failure in prod must be caused by a bug in the code.
exercises.explain: The code may be perfect; identity, permissions, catalog, schema, storage credential, configuration, secrets, compute or runtime may differ.

exercises.q: Which one is NOT among the dev-vs-prod differences listed in the lesson?
exercises.explain: The nine: identity, permissions, catalog, schema, storage credential, configuration, secret, compute, runtime.

exercises.q: Match each symptom to its first move.
pairs: Walk the layers from the source
Find where the second copy first appears
Works in dev, fails in prod
Walk the privilege path, then check run identity
exercises.explain: All four apply the same principle: find the first point where reality diverges from expectation.

exercises.q: Every symptom (missing data, duplicates, PERMISSION_DENIED) is itself a root cause you can fix directly.
exercises.explain: They are symptoms. The course's rule: find the first layer where reality diverges, and the mechanism there is the root cause.

exercises.q: Order the learning path that follows the prerequisites.
exercises.explain: The roadmap goes from the platform itself to storage (Delta), governance (UC), ingestion, pipelines, orchestration, SQL, performance and then Bundles/CI-CD, security, production projects and certification drills.

exercises.q: Which topic is part of 'Databricks — Part 1' in the roadmap?
exercises.explain: Part 1 covers the platform basics: account vs workspace, control vs compute plane, compute types, SQL warehouses, Runtime, Photon, notebooks and first debugging.
